deed: Raphael Mechoulam Isolates THC for the First Time
title: Isolating THC for the First Time

trailer.text: Raphael Mechoulam was an Israeli chemist and researcher, and according to the International Cannabinoid Research Society he is best known for his pioneering work in cannabis research.
He was born in Bulgaria in 1930 and immigrated with his family to Israel in 1949.
According to the World of Cannabis Museum, in 1962 Mechoulam asked for help obtaining hashish from the police for research.
According to the International Cannabinoid Research Society, his work paved the way for new drugs and treatments for chronic pain, epilepsy and multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs.text: According to Tablet, Raphael Mechoulam was born on November 5, 1930, in Sofia, Bulgaria, into a well-to-do Sephardic Jewish family.
His father was a physician and head of the Jewish hospital in Sofia.
In 1949 Mechoulam immigrated with his family to Israel, where he studied chemistry.
According to Tablet, he received a master's degree in biochemistry from the Hebrew University in 1952, and a doctorate from the Weizmann Institute in 1958.
His doctoral thesis dealt with the chemistry of steroids.
Mechoulam said that in a small country like Israel, anyone who wants to do significant work should try something new.

stations.title: A Plant No One Had Deciphered

paragraphs.text: When Mechoulam entered the field in the 1960s, morphine and cocaine had already been isolated from the opium and coca plants.
According to Mechoulam, the active compound in hashish had never yet been isolated in pure form.
According to the Jerusalem Post, in the 1960s cannabis was seen as an intoxicating drug with no medical benefits.
According to Mechoulam, the American NIH rejected his grant application, claiming the subject was not relevant because no one smokes marijuana in the U.S.

stations.title: Five Kilos of Hashish from the Police

paragraphs.text: According to the World of Cannabis Museum, in 1962 Mechoulam asked the director of the Weizmann Institute for help obtaining hashish from the police for research.
According to NPR, Mechoulam said that at first the team obtained the material for the research from the local police.
According to the World of Cannabis Museum, at a police station in Tel Aviv Mechoulam received five kilos of hashish that had been seized while being smuggled from Lebanon.
In the early 1960s Mechoulam carried five kilograms of hashish on a bus from Tel Aviv to Rehovot.
Later Mechoulam and the police learned that a request for illegal substances required a permit from the Ministry of Health, and that the transaction could have landed them in prison.
According to NPR, in 1962 Mechoulam and his team began to focus on the drug.
Mechoulam and his colleagues, Yehiel Gaoni and Haviv Edery, began an in-depth study of the compounds in hashish.
In the year after isolating CBD, the team succeeded in isolating THC and mapping its structure, using a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer.
According to Tablet, Mechoulam was the first in the world to isolate THC, the component of cannabis that causes the "high."
According to JNS, the team isolated some of the major compounds in marijuana, many of which had not been known before.
On April 1, 1964, the team published its findings in a paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.
Before publishing the findings, to confirm in humans that they had identified the right substance, Mechoulam took pure THC powder home and invited friends over for cake.
According to a scientific review published in PMC, Adams isolated CBD as a crystalline solid and also determined its molecular formula.

stations.title: From the Lab to the Patients

paragraphs.text: According to Mechoulam, NIH representatives came to Israel and took 10 grams of isolated THC back with them, and most of the initial research in the U.S. was done with this material.
According to Mechoulam, the NIH supported his work for almost 45 years.
In 1980 Mechoulam showed that CBD could treat seizures in epilepsy patients.
According to Mechoulam, for 35 years nothing happened with CBD, until parents discovered that it helps their children with epilepsy.
GW Pharmaceuticals developed Epidiolex, the first plant-based cannabis drug, which was approved in the U.S. in 2018.
Israel's Ministry of Health first approved the use of medical cannabis in 1992.

According to the Jerusalem Post, in an article on Meshulam's death, there were at that time more than 110,000 medical cannabis license holders in Israel, according to data from the medical cannabis unit operating within the Ministry of Health.
According to the World of Cannabis Museum, thanks to the work of Mechoulam and his team, Israel became a global leader in medical cannabis research.

stations.title: A Whole System Inside the Body

paragraphs.text: According to the World of Cannabis Museum, the first endocannabinoid was discovered in December 1992.
According to Eddy Portnoy, Mechoulam and his colleagues discovered the endocannabinoid system in the 1990s.
Mechoulam was a pioneer in the study of this system, which produces chemicals similar to THC in the body to regulate appetite, pain and the immune system.
According to Tablet, in 2019 Mechoulam was researching compounds of the body related to anandamide, which he had discovered more than 20 years earlier.
According to Mechoulam, anandamide had never yet been given to humans as a drug.

According to Discover, human trials of cannabinoid acids, which Mechoulam supplies for the development of treatments in partnership with the company EPM, to treat psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease were scheduled to begin the year after the interview.
According to the World of Cannabis Museum, Mechoulam and his team identified and synthesized more than 100 compounds, among them CBG and CBC.
In 1998, Mechoulam was the first to propose the concept of the so-called entourage effect.
In 1993 Mechoulam and his team published in Nature an analysis of ashes from a 4th-century Roman tomb of a young woman who died in childbirth.
The analysis confirmed his hypothesis and provided the first physical evidence of cannabis use in the ancient Middle East.
Mechoulam became a full professor at the Hebrew University in 1972, and in 1975 he received the Lionel Jacobson Chair in Medicinal Chemistry.
In 1994 he was elected a member of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities.
In 2017 he helped found the Multidisciplinary Center for Cannabinoid Research at the Hebrew University.
According to the Jerusalem Post, Mechoulam won the Israel Prize in Exact Sciences in the field of chemistry, and the Technion's Harvey Prize.
According to the World of Cannabis Museum, he published nearly 400 scientific articles and received several honorary degrees.
His 90th birthday was marked in 2021 at the closing event of the 31st International Cannabinoid Research Symposium, which was held online.
Mechoulam died on March 9, 2023, at the age of 92, at his home in Jerusalem.
His funeral was set for Sunday, March 12, at the Jerusalem Community Funeral Home in Givat Shaul, Jerusalem.
The president of the Hebrew University, Asher Cohen, said that most of the human and scientific knowledge about cannabis was accumulated thanks to Prof. Mechoulam.
The International Cannabinoid Research Society's 2023 Mechoulam Award was the 24th award bearing his name.
Mechoulam regretted that strict drug laws in the U.S. and elsewhere halted research and kept cannabis-derived drugs off the market.
According to Mechoulam, approval for a CBD drug could have been given 35 years earlier, and thousands of children could have been helped.
According to the Jerusalem Post, cannabis research was easier to conduct in Israel than in the U.S., which restricted it more.
In 2017 Mechoulam told the New York Times that Israel had more clinical trials than the U.S., and called it ridiculous.
There were difficulties in Israel too: according to Rick Doblin, Israeli patients complained about bureaucracy at the Ministry of Health regarding medical cannabis.
